etymology: From Saxon ploh; the Authorized Version prints both plow and plough. Webster 1828: to turn up, break, or till the ground with a plough. Scripture uses it of diligence, of the sluggard, of sowing wickedness, and of the man who looks back.
biblical_def: Plow in Scripture is the labour that must be done before anything can grow, and it is used to test a man in four ways. Proverbs tests his diligence: The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and have nothing (Proverbs 20:4) — the cold is real, the excuse is reasonable, and the harvest is empty. Hosea tests his moral sowing: Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity; ye have eaten the fruit of lies: because thou didst trust in thy way, in the multitude of thy mighty men (Hosea 10:13). Wickedness is not merely committed but cultivated, and the crop comes up. Paul tests the churches’ obligation to their ministers, applying the ox-and-corn law of Deuteronomy: he that ploweth should plow in hope; and that he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope (1 Corinthians 9:10). And the Lord tests a would-be disciple’s attachment to what he is leaving: No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62) — spoken to a man who asked only to go home and say farewell.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PLOW (also written PLOUGH) as to turn up, break, or till the ground with a plough; and figuratively, to furrow, to run through, or to labour with painful effort.
webster_full: PLOW, v.t. — To turn up, break, or till the ground with a plough, for the purpose of sowing.
To furrow; to make furrows or ridges in; to divide, as a ship ploughs the sea.
PLOW, n. — An instrument for turning up and preparing the soil for the reception of seed.
Figuratively, to labour with painful effort, or to prepare the way for what is to follow.
From Saxon ploh; the Authorized Version prints both plow and plough in different places.
scriptures: Proverbs 20:4
The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and have nothing.
Hosea 10:13
Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity; ye have eaten the fruit of lies: because thou didst trust in thy way, in the multitude of thy mighty men.
1 Corinthians 9:10
Or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this is written: that he that ploweth should plow in hope; and that he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope.
Luke 9:62
And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Luke 9:62 is spoken to a man whose request — to say farewell to his household — was entirely reasonable, and the Lord’s refusal to soften it stands against a discipleship offered on terms the hearer sets.
corruption_paragraphs: Three men come to Christ in the last verses of Luke 9 and none of them is handled the way modern practice would handle them. The first volunteers to follow anywhere and is told the Son of man has nowhere to lay His head. The second is called and asks first to bury his father. The third asks only to bid farewell to those at home — the very thing Elisha was permitted when Elijah cast his mantle on him — and receives the plough saying. The Lord is not indifferent to family; He commanded honour to parents and provided for His mother from the cross. He is refusing to let the call be renegotiated after it has been given. Ploughing with the head turned produces a crooked furrow, and a discipleship that keeps looking back at what it left will produce nothing straight.

Hosea 10:13 supplies the agricultural principle underneath, and it is the one modern moral thinking most consistently denies. Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity. Sin is not merely an act with consequences attached from outside; it is a sowing, and it grows a crop of its own kind. Paul states it flatly: Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap (Galatians 6:7). Proverbs 20:4 shows the same law in the ordinary business of a farm, and it is a mercy that it does: the man who will not work in the cold begs in the harvest, and no one has to explain the connection to him.
roots_summary: Hebrew charash (H2790), to plow, to engrave, and also to be silent; machareshah (H4281), a plowshare; Greek arotriao (G722), to plow; arotron (G723), a plough.
roots_lines: Hebrew charash (H2790) — to cut in, to plow, to engrave; the same root means to devise, as one who deviseth mischief.
Hebrew machareshah (H4281) — a plowshare; they shall beat their swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4).
Greek arotriao (G722) — to plow; he that ploweth should plow in hope (1 Corinthians 9:10).
Greek arotron (G723) — a plough; only at Luke 9:62.
Hebrew nir (H5215) — tilled ground, a fallow field; Break up your fallow ground (Hosea 10:12).
usage: The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold (Proverbs 20:4) — a real cold, a reasonable excuse, and an empty harvest.
Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity (Hosea 10:13) — sin cultivated, and the crop coming up.
Having put his hand to the plough, and looking back (Luke 9:62) — a call that may not be renegotiated.

etymology: From rear, Saxon raeran, to raise. Webster 1828: raised; lifted up; erected; brought up or educated. Scripture uses it of the tabernacle set up, of altars to Baal, and of a monument a man raised to his own name.
biblical_def: Reared means raised or set up, and Scripture applies it to three very different erections. It is used of the tabernacle, assembled exactly as God commanded on the first day of the second year: And Moses reared up the tabernacle, and fastened his sockets, and set up the boards thereof, and put in the bars thereof, and reared up his pillars (Exodus 40:18). It is used of the altars of apostasy: he reared up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria (1 Kings 16:32) of Ahab, and of Manasseh, he built up again the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed; and he reared up altars for Baal, and made a grove, as did Ahab king of Israel; and worshipped all the host of heaven (2 Kings 21:3) — a son deliberately undoing his father’s reformation. And it is used of a monument to a man’s own name: Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king’s dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance; and he called the pillar after his own name (2 Samuel 18:18) — erected by a man who had three sons, and who died in a tree.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REARED as raised; lifted up; set upright; erected, as a building or a pillar; and, of children and animals, brought up, nursed, or educated.
webster_full: REARED, pp. — Raised; lifted up; set upright; erected.
Brought up; educated; nursed and trained, as a child or an animal.
REAR, v.t. — To raise; to lift up; to set upright; to erect, as a building or a monument.
To bring to maturity; to breed and nourish; as, to rear cattle or to rear a family.
From Saxon raeran, to raise — a causative form of rise.
scriptures: Exodus 40:18
And Moses reared up the tabernacle, and fastened his sockets, and set up the boards thereof, and put in the bars thereof, and reared up his pillars.
1 Kings 16:32
And he reared up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he had built in Samaria.
2 Kings 21:3

For he built up again the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed; and he reared up altars for Baal, and made a grove, as did Ahab king of Israel; and worshipped all the host of heaven, and served them.
2 Samuel 18:18

Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king's dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance: and he called the pillar after his own name: and it is called unto this day, Absalom's place.
corruption_summary: 2 Kings 21:3 records a son systematically rebuilding what his father had torn down, which is the standing warning that a reformation is never more than one generation from being reversed.
corruption_paragraphs: Hezekiah had removed the high places, broken the images, cut down the groves, and destroyed the brasen serpent Moses had made when Israel began burning incense to it. Manasseh, his son, built up again the high places which Hezekiah his father had destroyed, reared altars for Baal, made a grove, worshipped the host of heaven, set a carved image in the house of the LORD, and made his son pass through the fire. The chapter says he made Judah do worse than the nations God had destroyed before them. No reformation is self-perpetuating. The Reformers understood this and built catechisms, household instruction, and confessions precisely because the recovery of the gospel in one generation guarantees nothing about the next. Deuteronomy 6 puts the duty in the home, at every hour of the day, and Judges 2:10 records what happens when it lapses: there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD.

Absalom’s pillar is the smaller and sadder text. He reared it for himself, in the king’s dale, because I have no son to keep my name in remembrance — and 2 Samuel 14:27 says he had three sons and a daughter. Whether they had died or whether he simply judged them insufficient, the monument was self-commissioned and self-named, and the man who built it was buried under a heap of stones in a wood. The contrast with Exodus 40:18 is the whole lesson of the entry: Moses reared up a structure whose pattern he had been given and whose glory he did not claim, and the cloud covered it and the glory of the LORD filled it. What a man rears to his own name is a pillar; what he rears at God’s command is filled.
roots_summary: Hebrew qum (H6965), to arise, to raise up; natsab (H5324), to set up, to station; banah (H1129), to build; Greek egeiro (G1453), to raise up.
roots_lines: Hebrew qum (H6965) — to arise, to stand, and causatively to raise up; Moses reared up the tabernacle (Exodus 40:18).
Hebrew natsab (H5324) — to station, to set up; reared up for himself a pillar (2 Samuel 18:18).
Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build; the companion verb in 1 Kings 16:32 and 2 Kings 21:3.
Hebrew matstsebah (H4676) — a standing pillar; used both of Jacob’s memorial at Bethel and of pagan sacred stones.
Greek egeiro (G1453) — to raise up; in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19).
usage: Moses reared up the tabernacle (Exodus 40:18) — built to a given pattern, and filled with glory.
He reared up altars for Baal (2 Kings 21:3) — a son undoing his father’s reformation, item by item.
Absalom… reared up for himself a pillar (2 Samuel 18:18) — self-commissioned, self-named, and buried under stones.

etymology: From speckle, a small spot, from Saxon specca. Webster 1828: marked with small spots of a different colour. Scripture uses it of Laban’s flocks in the account of Jacob’s wages, of a bird set upon by others, and of the horses of Zechariah’s first vision.
biblical_def: Speckled means marked with spots of another colour, and its principal use is the strangest wage negotiation in Scripture. Jacob proposes to take as his hire only the irregular animals: I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire (Genesis 30:32). Laban changes the terms repeatedly, and Jacob later tells his wives how it went: If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages; then all the cattle bare speckled: and if he said thus, The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked (Genesis 31:8). Whatever Laban named, the flocks produced — and Jacob attributes it not to his rods in the watering troughs but to God, who hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me. Jeremiah uses the word of a nation marked out for attack: Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her (Jeremiah 12:9). And Zechariah sees speckled horses among the patrol that walks the earth (Zechariah 1:8).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SPECKLED as marked with specks; variegated with spots of a different colour from the ground or surface.
webster_full: SPECKLED, a. — Marked with specks; variegated with spots of a different colour from the ground.
SPECKLE, n. — A small spot in anything of a different substance or colour from that of the thing itself.
Applied in Scripture chiefly to cattle, goats, sheep, birds, and horses.
Distinguished from ringstraked, marked with rings or bands, and from spotted, marked with larger patches.
From Saxon specca, a spot — the root also of speck and speckle.
scriptures: Genesis 30:32

I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire.
Genesis 31:8
If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages; then all the cattle bare speckled: and if he said thus, The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked.
Jeremiah 12:9
Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird, the birds round about are against her; come ye, assemble all the beasts of the field, come to devour.
Zechariah 1:8
I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were there red horses, speckled, and white.
corruption_summary: The rods in the watering troughs are sometimes read as a piece of folk breeding-magic that Scripture endorses, when the narrative itself credits God and Jacob says so plainly to his wives.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 30 records what Jacob did — peeled rods of poplar, hazel and chestnut set in the gutters where the flocks came to drink — without saying it worked. Genesis 31 gives the explanation, and it comes from Jacob’s own mouth and from an angel in a dream: God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me, and the angel says I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee. Scripture frequently narrates what men did without endorsing it; the polygamy of the patriarchs is reported in the same manner. The lesson of the chapter is providence overruling a decade of a cheat’s manoeuvres — Laban changed Jacob’s wages ten times, and every change was answered from heaven before Jacob could think of a device.

Jeremiah 12:9 turns the image against God’s own people, and the pastoral point is worth naming. A speckled bird in a flock of plain ones is attacked by the rest for being unlike them, and God says His heritage has become such a bird. Judah’s distinctness, which should have been her glory as the people bearing God’s name, had become the mark that drew the beasts. The chapter is Jeremiah’s complaint that the wicked prosper and God’s answer that harder things are coming — if thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? A church distinct from its neighbours should expect the treatment of the speckled bird, and should not conclude from it that God has abandoned His heritage.
roots_summary: Hebrew naqod (H5348), speckled, marked with points; taluw (H2921), spotted; aqod (H6124), ringstraked, banded; tsabua (H6641), coloured, speckled — the word of Jeremiah 12:9.
roots_lines: Hebrew naqod (H5348) — speckled, marked with points; the term of Jacob’s wages (Genesis 30:32).
Hebrew aqod (H6124) — ringstraked, marked with bands at the ankles; the alternative Laban proposed.
Hebrew taluw (H2921) — spotted, patched; the third category in the same negotiation.
Hebrew tsabua (H6641) — coloured, variegated; as a speckled bird (Jeremiah 12:9).
Hebrew barod (H1261) — grisled, dappled; the speckled horses of Zechariah 1:8 and 6:3.
usage: Of such shall be my hire (Genesis 30:32) — a wage taken only from the irregular animals.
If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages; then all the cattle bare speckled (Genesis 31:8) — every change of terms answered from heaven.
Mine heritage is unto me as a speckled bird (Jeremiah 12:9) — distinctness that draws the flock’s attack.

etymology: From saddle, Saxon sadel. Webster 1828: covered with a saddle; furnished with a saddle. In Scripture the word marks the moment a man sets out, and it is used at two of the most consequential departures in the Old Testament.
biblical_def: Saddled is a small word that Scripture places at the head of great journeys. The greatest is Abraham’s: And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son, and clave the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him (Genesis 22:3). Seven verbs in one verse, and not one word of protest, argument, or explanation — a man who had waited twenty-five years for the son now cutting the wood to burn him. The narrative gives us his obedience and withholds his thoughts, and Hebrews 11:19 supplies what he was reasoning: that God was able to raise Isaac from the dead. The word marks another early rising with the opposite spirit: And Balaam rose up in the morning, and saddled his ass, and went with the princes of Moab (Numbers 22:21) — a prophet setting out on an errand God had permitted rather than commanded, and God’s anger was kindled because he went. And it marks the errand of the old prophet who went after the man of God and lied to him: And he said unto his sons, Saddle me the ass. So they saddled him the ass: and he rode thereon (1 Kings 13:13).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SADDLED as covered with a saddle; furnished with a saddle; and figuratively, loaded or burdened with something to be borne.
webster_full: SADDLED, pp. — Covered or furnished with a saddle, as a beast for riding.
Loaded; burdened; as, saddled with a debt or an encumbrance.
SADDLE, n. — A seat to be placed on a horse’s or an ass’s back for the rider.
SADDLE, v.t. — To put a saddle on; and hence, to fix a burden or charge upon.
From Saxon sadel — connected with sit and with the Latin sedeo, to sit.
scriptures: Genesis 22:3

And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son, and clave the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him.
Numbers 22:21
And Balaam rose up in the morning, and saddled his ass, and went with the princes of Moab.
1 Kings 13:13
And he said unto his sons, Saddle me the ass. So they saddled him the ass: and he rode thereon,
2 Samuel 19:26
And he answered, My lord, O king, my servant deceived me: for thy servant said, I will saddle me an ass, that I may ride thereon, and go to the king; because thy servant is lame.
corruption_summary: Genesis 22 is regularly softened into a story about a test God never intended to complete, or condemned outright as divine cruelty, and both readings avoid what the New Testament says the chapter is for.
corruption_paragraphs: The account is not offered as a general model for how God deals with fathers and sons; it is a single, unrepeatable command, given to the man through whom the promised seed was to come, and it is stopped by God Himself. Hebrews 11:17-19 tells us what was in Abraham’s mind: he accounted that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead, having been told that in Isaac shall thy seed be called. So Abraham reasoned from the promise, not against it. And the chapter’s deepest purpose is typological: a father and an only son, a three-day journey, wood carried by the son up the hill, the son asking where the lamb is, the answer God will provide himself a lamb, a substitute caught in a thicket, and a place named Jehovah-jireh on the mountain where the temple would later stand. What God did not require of Abraham He did not spare Himself: He that spared not his own Son (Romans 8:32).

Numbers 22:21 is the necessary counterweight. Balaam also rose early and saddled his ass, and God’s anger was kindled because he went — although God had said go with them. The distinction is between a permission wrung out of God by a man who kept asking, and a command. Balaam had already been told plainly, Thou shalt not go with them; thou shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed, and he asked again. Scripture treats a permission obtained by persistence as a dangerous thing to hold, and Psalm 106:15 describes the same pattern in Israel: he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul.
roots_summary: Hebrew chabash (H2280), to bind on, to saddle, to bind up a wound; merkab (H4817), a saddle, a chariot seat; Greek epibaino (G1910), to mount, to go aboard.
roots_lines: Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind on, to gird; used both of saddling a beast and of binding up the brokenhearted (Isaiah 61:1).
Hebrew merkab (H4817) — a saddle or seat for riding; whatsoever saddle he rideth upon (Leviticus 15:9).
Hebrew athon (H860) — a she-ass; the beast Abraham and Balaam both saddled.
Greek epibaino (G1910) — to mount, to embark; used of Christ riding into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:5).
Hebrew shakam (H7925) — to rise early; the verb that opens both Genesis 22:3 and Numbers 22:21.
usage: Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his ass (Genesis 22:3) — seven verbs of obedience, and no protest recorded.
Balaam rose up in the morning, and saddled his ass (Numbers 22:21) — the same early rising on a permitted errand, and God’s anger kindled.
Saddle me the ass. So they saddled him the ass (1 Kings 13:13) — an old prophet setting out to lie to a younger one.

etymology: From Saxon cu. Webster 1828: the female of the bovine genus. Scripture uses the word of the prosperity of the wicked, of the poverty of a stripped land, and of the peace of the restored creation.
biblical_def: Cow appears rarely in the Authorized Version, which usually prefers kine, heifer, or ox, and where it appears it carries weight. Job uses it in the passage that states the problem of the prospering wicked more sharply than any modern sceptic: Their bull gendereth, and faileth not; their cow calveth, and casteth not her calf (Job 21:10). Their herds breed without loss, their children dance, they spend their days in wealth and go down to the grave in a moment — and Job says so to friends who had insisted that suffering tracks sin. Isaiah uses it to describe a land so stripped that a man’s whole estate is one animal and two sheep: it shall come to pass in that day, that a man shall nourish a young cow, and two sheep (Isaiah 7:21). And Isaiah uses it in the great picture of the restored creation, where the predator and the prey are pastured together: And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox (Isaiah 11:7). The passage begins with the rod out of the stem of Jesse, and the peace of the animals follows from the reign of the Branch.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines COW as the female of the bovine genus of quadrupeds; the male being called a bull, and the young a calf. The Authorized Version more often uses kine for the plural.
webster_full: COW, n. — The female of the bovine genus of quadrupeds; the male is called a bull, and the young a calf.
The plural in the Authorized Version is usually kine, an older form still preserved in Scripture.
HEIFER, n. — A young cow that has not borne a calf; the animal of the red heifer ordinance.
Cattle generally were reckoned among the chief measures of a household’s wealth in the patriarchal age.
From Saxon cu, plural cy, whence kine — cognate with the German Kuh.
scriptures: Their bull gendereth, and faileth not; their cow calveth, and casteth not her calf.
Isaiah 7:21
And it shall come to pass in that day, that a man shall nourish a young cow, and two sheep;
Isaiah 11:7
And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox.
Numbers 19:2

This is the ordinance of the law which the LORD hath commanded, saying, Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring thee a red heifer without spot, wherein is no blemish, and upon which never came yoke:
corruption_summary: Job 21 states the prosperity of the wicked without softening it, and both the retribution theology of Job’s friends and the modern prosperity teaching make the same error from opposite ends: they read a man’s circumstances as a verdict on his standing with God.
corruption_paragraphs: Job’s answer in chapter 21 is a direct assault on his friends’ doctrine, and it is in the canon. Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power? Their houses are safe from fear, their bull breeds without failing, their cow calves without loss, their children dance, they say to God Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways — and they die easily. Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar had built everything on the rule that the righteous prosper and the wicked suffer, and God says at the end that they had not spoken of Him the thing that was right. The prosperity gospel is the same equation run forward: if the equation held, Job 21 could not have been written and the cross could not have happened.

Isaiah 11:7 supplies the answer that the book of Job leaves for later revelation. The resolution is not a formula that explains present suffering but a coming order under a coming King — the rod out of the stem of Jesse, the Spirit resting upon Him, judgment for the poor with righteousness, and then the wolf with the lamb, the cow and the bear feeding, the lion eating straw. The dictionary reads this as genuinely eschatological, fulfilled in the new heavens and new earth, and its ground is stated in verse 9: the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea. Job’s question is answered by a Person and a kingdom, not by an explanation.
roots_summary: Hebrew parah (H6510), a cow, a heifer; par (H6499), a bullock; baqar (H1241), a herd, cattle; eglah (H5697), a heifer.
roots_lines: Hebrew parah (H6510) — a cow, a heifer; the red heifer of Numbers 19:2 is parah adummah.
Hebrew par (H6499) — a young bull, a bullock; the chief sin offering of the priest (Leviticus 4:3).
Hebrew baqar (H1241) — cattle, a herd; the ordinary word for the larger livestock of a household.
Hebrew eglah (H5697) — a heifer; the heifer that is beheaded in the rite of Deuteronomy 21:4.
Hebrew shakal (H7921) — to be bereaved, to miscarry; casteth not her calf (Job 21:10).
usage: Their cow calveth, and casteth not her calf (Job 21:10) — the prosperity of the wicked, stated without softening.
A man shall nourish a young cow, and two sheep (Isaiah 7:21) — a whole estate reduced to three animals.
The cow and the bear shall feed (Isaiah 11:7) — the peace of creation under the reign of the Branch.

etymology: From Saxon taegel. Webster 1828: the part of an animal which terminates its body behind; the hinder or lower part of anything. Scripture uses it in a sign given to Moses, in a covenant blessing, in Samson’s revenge, and in a prophetic rebuke.
biblical_def: Tail in Scripture is nearly always the low end of something, and the images built on it are memorable. God’s first sign to Moses is given at the dangerous end of a serpent: Put forth thine hand, and take it by the tail. And he put forth his hand, and caught it, and it became a rod in his hand (Exodus 4:4) — a man is told to seize a snake exactly where a man never would, and obedience turns the serpent back into a staff. The covenant blessings use head and tail for a nation’s standing among others: the LORD shall make thee the head, and not the tail; and thou shalt be above only, and thou shalt not be beneath; if that thou hearken unto the commandments of the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 28:13), with the curse in verse 44 reversing it exactly. Isaiah applies the figure inside the nation and names who the tail is: The ancient and honourable, he is the head; and the prophet that teacheth lies, he is the tail (Isaiah 9:15). And Samson’s revenge on the Philistine harvest is executed by it: Samson went and caught three hundred foxes, and took firebrands, and turned tail to tail, and put a firebrand in the midst between two tails (Judges 15:4).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TAIL as the part of an animal which terminates its body behind; and, by extension, the hinder, lower, or concluding part of anything — opposed to the head.
webster_full: TAIL, n. — The part of an animal which terminates its body behind.
The lower or hinder part of anything; the conclusion or extremity.
Figuratively, the lowest or most despised part; opposed to the head, which signifies pre-eminence.
In Scripture, the head and the tail together express the whole of a people, from the highest to the lowest.
From Saxon taegel — the root also of tailings and of entail in its legal sense of a cut-off estate.
scriptures: Exodus 4:4
And the LORD said unto Moses, Put forth thine hand, and take it by the tail. And he put forth his hand, and caught it, and it became a rod in his hand:
Deuteronomy 28:13

And the LORD shall make thee the head, and not the tail; and thou shalt be above only, and thou shalt not be beneath; if that thou hearken unto the commandments of the LORD thy God, which I command thee this day, to observe and to do them:
Isaiah 9:15
The ancient and honourable, he is the head; and the prophet that teacheth lies, he is the tail.
Judges 15:4
And Samson went and caught three hundred foxes, and took firebrands, and turned tail to tail, and put a firebrand in the midst between two tails.
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 28:13 is a favourite text of prosperity preaching, lifted out of a covenant made with a particular nation and turned into a promise of personal advancement, with the conditions and the matching curses left unread.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 28 is one chapter with two halves. Fourteen verses of blessing are followed by fifty-four of curse, and both are conditional on obedience to a covenant made with Israel at Sinai. Verse 13 promises the head and not the tail if that thou hearken unto the commandments of the LORD thy God; verse 44 threatens that the stranger shall be the head and Israel the tail. Preaching that claims verse 13 for a believer’s finances while ignoring verse 44, and while dropping the condition, is not applying the text but harvesting it. The New Testament does apply the Mosaic covenant to the church, but through Christ, who redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and the blessing promised there is that the blessing of Abraham should come on the Gentiles — namely, the promise of the Spirit.

Isaiah 9:15 shows the figure used with far more edge, and it names names. The head is the ancient and honourable; the tail is the prophet that teacheth lies. God ranks a lying prophet at the bottom of the nation, and the preceding verse says the LORD will cut off head and tail in one day. Isaiah is not attacking prophecy but false prophecy, and his verdict is more severe than modern discourse permits: a teacher who tells the people what they wish to hear is not a well-meaning colleague with a different emphasis but the tail of the nation, and verse 16 adds that they that are led of them are destroyed.
roots_summary: Hebrew zanab (H2180), a tail; rosh (H7218), a head; Greek oura (G3769), a tail; Hebrew shual (H7776), a fox or jackal.
roots_lines: Hebrew zanab (H2180) — a tail; as a verb, to cut off the rear of an army (Deuteronomy 25:18).
Hebrew rosh (H7218) — a head, a chief; the contrasting term throughout Deuteronomy 28.
Hebrew shual (H7776) — a fox or jackal; the three hundred of Judges 15:4.
Greek oura (G3769) — a tail; used of the locusts and the horses of Revelation 9.
Hebrew lappid (H3940) — a torch, a firebrand; the brands Samson bound between the tails.
usage: Take it by the tail… and it became a rod in his hand (Exodus 4:4) — a serpent seized where no man would seize one.
The LORD shall make thee the head, and not the tail (Deuteronomy 28:13) — a covenant promise with a stated condition and a matching curse.
The prophet that teacheth lies, he is the tail (Isaiah 9:15) — God’s ranking of a false prophet in the nation.

etymology: From Old French escale, a husk or shell. Webster 1828: the small shells or crusts which cover the skin of fishes and reptiles; also a thin lamina or flake. Distinct from scales the balance, which is from a different root.
biblical_def: Scales in Scripture are the plates that cover a fish or a monster, and the word appears in the food law, in the description of leviathan, and at the conversion of Paul. The dietary law makes them a test: whatsoever hath fins and scales in the waters, in the seas, and in the rivers, them shall ye eat (Leviticus 11:9), repeated at Deuteronomy 14:9. Fins and scales together mark a creature that keeps to its own element and moves through it in the ordered way; without both it was unclean to Israel. Job’s description of leviathan makes the scales an image of impenetrable pride: His scales are his pride, shut up together as with a close seal (Job 41:15) — a creature so armoured that no weapon reaches it, produced by God as the last argument in the whirlwind. And Luke uses the word for the moment Saul of Tarsus received his sight: immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized (Acts 9:18). The man who had been struck blind by the light of Christ’s glory sees again when Ananias, a disciple of the sect he had come to destroy, lays hands on him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SCALE as the small shell or crust which composes a part of the covering of a fish or reptile; also, a thin lamina or flake. Webster distinguishes this word from scale, a balance, and scale, a ladder or graduated series.
webster_full: SCALE, n. — The small shell or crust which forms part of the covering of a fish or a reptile.
A thin plate or lamina; a flake; anything resembling a fish’s scale in thinness and overlap.
Webster keeps this word distinct from SCALE, a balance for weighing, and from SCALE, a ladder or a graduated line.
In the Levitical law, fins and scales together were the mark of a clean water creature.
From Old French escale, a husk or shell — the root also of shell and scallop.
scriptures: Leviticus 11:9
These shall ye eat of all that are in the waters: whatsoever hath fins and scales in the waters, in the seas, and in the rivers, them shall ye eat.
Deuteronomy 14:9
These ye shall eat of all that are in the waters: all that have fins and scales shall ye eat:
His scales are his pride, shut up together as with a close seal.
Acts 9:18
And immediately there fell from his eyes as it had been scales: and he received sight forthwith, and arose, and was baptized.
corruption_summary: The food laws are frequently offered as evidence that Scripture’s commands are arbitrary or merely hygienic, and both readings miss the stated purpose, which is to teach a people to distinguish.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 11 gives its own reason at the end of the chapter: to make a difference between the unclean and the clean, because I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy. The laws trained a nation in discrimination — in the daily habit of asking what belongs to God’s people and what does not — and they marked Israel out visibly from every neighbour, since a nation that cannot eat with its neighbours will not intermarry with them either. The hygienic explanation is not the point and does not fit all the cases. And the arbitrariness objection misses that the ceremonial law was never permanent: Christ declared all meats clean (Mark 7:19), Peter was taught it on a rooftop, and the dictionary holds with the confession that the ceremonial laws are now abrogated while the moral law abides.

Acts 9:18 has been so worn by devotional use that its actual shape is worth restating. The scales did not fall from the eyes of a man who was groping toward the truth; they fell from a man who had been blinded for three days after meeting the risen Christ on a road he was travelling with warrants to arrest Christians. He did not reason his way in. He was struck down, named, blinded, and led by the hand into the city, and his sight was restored by a frightened disciple who had argued with God about going. That is what the Reformed tradition means by effectual calling, and Paul spent the rest of his life describing himself as one born out of due time and the least of the apostles because of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew qasqeseth (H7193), a scale of a fish; magen (H4043), a shield — used of leviathan’s scales; Greek lepis (G3013), a scale, a flake; pterugion, a fin.
roots_lines: Hebrew qasqeseth (H7193) — a fish scale; the term of Leviticus 11:9 and Deuteronomy 14:9.
Hebrew magen (H4043) — a shield; leviathan’s scales are literally his shields, shut up together as with a close seal (Job 41:15).
Greek lepis (G3013) — a scale, a flake; only at Acts 9:18.
Hebrew senappir (H5579) — a fin; the companion requirement to scales in the clean-creature test.
Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, to separate; the verb of the law’s stated purpose, to make a difference.
usage: Whatsoever hath fins and scales… them shall ye eat (Leviticus 11:9) — a law that trained a nation to distinguish.
His scales are his pride, shut up together as with a close seal (Job 41:15) — armour no weapon reaches.
There fell from his eyes as it had been scales (Acts 9:18) — sight restored to a man struck blind on his way to arrest Christians.

etymology: From Saxon ripe, mature, ready for reaping. Webster 1828: brought to perfection in growth; mature; fit for use. Scripture uses it of grapes in a dream, of the season for gathering, and twice of a wickedness ready for the sickle.
biblical_def: Ripe means ready, and Scripture uses the word most solemnly of a wickedness that has come to full growth. Joel gives the command over the valley of decision: Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great (Joel 3:13) — and the ripeness in view is not corn but iniquity, which had to fill up before judgment fell. Revelation takes up the same figure at the end: Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe (Revelation 14:15). The word also carries God’s ordinary providence. The spies are sent at exactly the right season: Now the time was the time of the firstripe grapes (Numbers 13:20), so that they returned carrying a cluster on a staff between two men — evidence of a good land, brought back by ten men who reported that it could not be taken. And Pharaoh’s butler dreams the vine that restores him: in the vine were three branches: and it was as though it budded, and her blossoms shot forth; and the clusters thereof brought forth ripe grapes (Genesis 40:10).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RIPE as brought to perfection in growth or maturity; mature; fit for use; and figuratively, advanced to the point of readiness, whether for good or for ill.
webster_full: RIPE, a. — Brought to perfection in growth; mature; fit for use, as fruit or grain.
Advanced to perfection; complete; finished; as, ripe in judgment or ripe in years.
Ready for action or for an event; as, a plot ripe for execution.
Resembling ripe fruit; hence, in Scripture, a wickedness come to its full and ready for judgment.
From Saxon ripe, mature — the root also of reap and ripen.
scriptures: Joel 3:13
Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great.
Revelation 14:15

And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to him that sat on the cloud, Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe.
Numbers 13:20

And what the land is, whether it be fat or lean, whether there be wood therein, or not. And be ye of good courage, and bring of the fruit of the land. Now the time was the time of the firstripe grapes.
Genesis 40:10
And in the vine were three branches: and it was as though it budded, and her blossoms shot forth; and the clusters thereof brought forth ripe grapes:
corruption_summary: Scripture teaches that God delays judgment until an iniquity is full, which answers both the complaint that He acts too soon and the assumption that His patience means He will never act at all.
corruption_paragraphs: God told Abraham that his descendants would not possess Canaan for four hundred years, and gave the reason: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full (Genesis 15:16). Four centuries of divine patience toward a people whose religion included child sacrifice, and the conquest waits until the ripening is complete. Joel 3:13 and Revelation 14:15 describe the moment the sickle finally goes in. This is the answer to the objection that the God of the conquest is arbitrary or hasty; the difficulty in the text, if any, runs entirely the other way. Peter states the principle for the present age: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise… but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). Patience is real, and it is not permanent.

Numbers 13:20 supplies a quieter lesson about seeing rightly. God sent the spies at the season of the firstripe grapes, so that the evidence would be unmistakable: they came back with a cluster so large it was carried on a staff between two men, and with figs and pomegranates. Ten of them then reported that the land ate up its inhabitants and that they were as grasshoppers in their own sight. The fruit in their hands did not change their report. Unbelief is not usually a shortage of evidence; it is a settled way of reading the evidence one already has, and Caleb and Joshua saw the same grapes and the same giants and drew the opposite conclusion.
roots_summary: Hebrew bashal (H1310), to boil, to ripen; bikkurah (H1073), the firstripe fig; qayits (H7019), summer fruit; Greek xeraino (G3583), to dry, to be ripe.
roots_lines: Hebrew bashal (H1310) — to boil or to ripen; the harvest is ripe (Joel 3:13).
Hebrew bikkurah (H1073) — the firstripe fig, the earliest and most prized; the time of the firstripe grapes (Numbers 13:20).
Hebrew qayits (H7019) — summer, summer fruit; Amos’s basket of summer fruit is a pun on qets, the end (Amos 8:2).
Greek xeraino (G3583) — to dry up, and so to be fully ripe; the harvest of the earth is ripe (Revelation 14:15).
Greek drepanon (G1407) — a sickle; the instrument in both Joel’s and John’s harvest.
usage: Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe (Joel 3:13) — and the crop in view is wickedness.
The harvest of the earth is ripe (Revelation 14:15) — the same figure at the end of the age.
Now the time was the time of the firstripe grapes (Numbers 13:20) — evidence carried home by men who would not believe it.

etymology: The past tense of spring, Saxon springan, to leap, to shoot up. Webster 1828: leaped; shot up; issued or proceeded from. Scripture uses it of seed on stony ground, of seed on good ground, of a nation from one dead man, and of the Lord’s descent from Judah.
biblical_def: Sprang is used of sudden growth, and the parable of the sower turns on the fact that sudden growth is not by itself a good sign. And some fell on stony ground, where it had not much earth; and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth (Mark 4:5) — and the speed is the symptom, not the promise; the shallow soil warms fastest and the plant that comes up quickest is the one that withers when the sun is up. The same verb describes the fourth soil, where the result is different: And other fell on good ground, and sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold (Luke 8:8). Hebrews uses it of a nation issuing from an old and childless couple: Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable (Hebrews 11:12). And it is used of the Lord’s tribal descent, in an argument about His priesthood: For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood (Hebrews 7:14) — He is a priest of another order entirely, after Melchisedec.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives SPRANG as the past tense of SPRING: leaped; bounded; shot up or forth, as a plant; issued or proceeded, as from a source or an ancestor.
webster_full: SPRANG, pret. of SPRING — Leaped; bounded; darted or shot forward.
Shot up; grew; as a plant issuing from the ground.
Issued or proceeded, as from a source, a stock, or an ancestor; as, he sprang from an ancient family.
Arose or came into being; as, a thought sprang up in the mind.
From Saxon springan, to leap — the root also of spring the season, and spring a fountain.
scriptures: Mark 4:5
And some fell on stony ground, where it had not much earth; and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth:
Luke 8:8
And other fell on good ground, and sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold. And when he had said these things, he cried, He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.
Hebrews 11:12
Therefore sprang there even of one, and him as good as dead, so many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as the sand which is by the sea shore innumerable.
Hebrews 7:14
For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood.
corruption_summary: Mark 4:5 makes rapid, joyful growth the mark of the stony-ground hearer rather than of the good-ground hearer, which is the reverse of the assumption on which most evangelistic follow-up operates.
corruption_paragraphs: The Lord’s own explanation is explicit: the stony-ground hearers when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with gladness; and have no root in themselves, and so endure but for a time: afterward, when affliction or persecution ariseth for the word’s sake, immediately they are offended. Two immediatelys frame the whole account — immediate reception and immediate offence — and the depth of the soil, not the speed of the shoot, decides everything. Modern evangelistic practice measures precisely the wrong variable: the immediate emotional response is counted, celebrated, and reported, while root is neither visible nor countable. Nothing here forbids joy at conversion; the good ground bears fruit too. It forbids treating the speed of the response as evidence of its reality.

Hebrews 7:14 uses the word in an argument of great weight for the doctrine of Christ’s priesthood. Our Lord sprang out of Judah, and Moses said nothing about priesthood for that tribe — the Levitical office belonged to Aaron’s line alone. Therefore His priesthood is not Aaronic but of another order, after Melchisedec, held not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life. That is why the Roman doctrine of a continuing sacrificing priesthood is an anachronism: the Levitical order has been superseded, and the one Priest who remains ever lives to make intercession. Hebrews 11:12 supplies the other note, and it is a mercy to anyone waiting: a nation as numerous as the stars sprang from one man who was as good as dead.
roots_summary: Greek anatello (G393), to rise, to spring up; phuo (G5453), to grow, to spring up; exanatello (G1816), to spring up out of; Hebrew tsamach (H6779), to sprout, to spring forth.
roots_lines: Greek exanatello (G1816) — to spring up out of; the quick shoot on stony ground (Mark 4:5).
Greek phuo (G5453) — to grow, to spring up; sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold (Luke 8:8).
Greek anatello (G393) — to rise, to spring; our Lord sprang out of Juda (Hebrews 7:14), with the messianic overtone of a rising branch.
Hebrew tsamach (H6779) — to sprout; the root of tsemach, the Branch, a messianic title (Zechariah 3:8).
Greek rhiza (G4491) — a root; have no root in themselves (Mark 4:17).
usage: Immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth (Mark 4:5) — the speed is the symptom, not the promise.
Sprang up, and bare fruit an hundredfold (Luke 8:8) — the same verb, and a different soil.
Our Lord sprang out of Juda (Hebrews 7:14) — a priesthood of another order altogether.

etymology: From parch, of uncertain origin, perhaps from Latin persiccare, to dry thoroughly. Webster 1828: scorched; dried to extremity by heat. Scripture uses it of ground without water, and of grain roasted at the fire — the ordinary food of harvesters and armies.
biblical_def: Parched in Scripture means dried by heat, and it names two things: land without water, and corn roasted over a fire. Of the land, Jeremiah gives the fate of the man who trusts in man: he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited (Jeremiah 17:6) — and the contrast four verses later is the tree planted by the waters, which does not see when heat cometh. Isaiah promises the reversal: the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes (Isaiah 35:7). Of the food, parched corn was what a reaper ate in the field, and Boaz hands it to a foreign widow gleaning behind his men: he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left (Ruth 2:14). And the law forbids eating it until the firstfruits have been offered: ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God (Leviticus 23:14).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PARCHED as scorched; dried to extremity by heat; and of grain, roasted or dried by the fire, as parched corn.
webster_full: PARCHED, pp. — Scorched; dried to extremity; deprived of moisture by heat.
Of grain, roasted or dried at the fire; as parched corn, a common food in the East.
Applied to land, denoting ground burnt dry and unfit for cultivation.
PARCH, v.t. — To burn the surface of; to scorch; to dry to extremity.
Of uncertain origin; perhaps from Latin persiccare, to dry thoroughly.
scriptures: Jeremiah 17:6
For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.
Isaiah 35:7
And the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes.
Ruth 2:14

And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left.
Leviticus 23:14

And ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God: it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah 17 sets trusting in man against trusting in the LORD and describes the first as a curse, which is the plainest biblical refutation of the therapeutic and political habit of locating a person’s hope in human help.
corruption_paragraphs: The passage is built as a pair. Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD — and he shall inhabit the parched places, in a salt land not inhabited, and shall not see when good comes. Then: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD… For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters… and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought. Both men face the same weather; one does not notice the good and the other does not notice the heat. Nothing here forbids the ordinary use of doctors, counsellors, friends, or magistrates — Scripture commends all of them. What it forbids is making flesh the arm, and Jeremiah adds the reason in the next breath: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?

Ruth 2:14 is one of the small kindnesses in Scripture that carries a large doctrine. Boaz calls a destitute Moabite widow to the reapers’ meal, seats her among his own workers, and hands her parched corn until she has eaten and left some over. She was outside the covenant by birth, poor, foreign, and gleaning by a legal charity she had no natural claim to. The man who fed her became her kinsman-redeemer, and their great-grandson was David. It is a picture worth setting against every account of grace as something earned or owed: the redeemer feeds the one he will redeem, before she knows what he intends.

roots_lines: Hebrew qali (H7039) — parched or roasted grain; the reapers’ food that Boaz gave to Ruth (Ruth 2:14).
Hebrew charer (H2787) — to be scorched, burned; behind the parched places in the wilderness (Jeremiah 17:6).
Hebrew sharab (H8273) — parched ground, and also the shimmering mirage of the desert; the parched ground shall become a pool (Isaiah 35:7).
Hebrew tsimmaon (H6774) — thirsty ground; the companion term in the same verse.
Hebrew melechah (H4420) — a salt land, barrenness; in a salt land and not inhabited (Jeremiah 17:6).
usage: He shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness (Jeremiah 17:6) — the man who makes flesh his arm.
The parched ground shall become a pool (Isaiah 35:7) — the promised reversal, in the habitation of dragons.
He reached her parched corn (Ruth 2:14) — a redeemer feeding the woman he would redeem.
